https://www.thetimes.com/article/dartfor.subtitle: Essex police chief constable calls protesters ‘crazy’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/dartfor.text:
The climate activists who shut a key bridge on the M25 have been removed by the police after causing two days of severe disruption.
The Queen Elizabeth II Bridge at the Dartford Crossing, connecting the M25 over the Thames between Essex and Kent, was closed when two protesters from the Just Stop Oil group climbed its 84m towers just before 4am on Monday.
The pair had vowed to continue the protest until the government made a “meaningful statement” promising to end all new licences for fossil fuel extraction. However, they agreed to co-operate with Essex police and end the protest at 5pm after the force brought in a specialist raised platform in the hope of convincing them to come down.
Just Stop Oil, which styles itself as a radical offshoot of Extinction Rebellion, identified one of the protesters as Morgan Trowland, 39, a bridge design engineer. The other is understood to be Marcus Carambola, 33, a teacher and musician.
In a statement, they said: “We successfully disrupted oil supplies to Kent and the southeast for 36 hours. We are stepping down now but other supporters of Just Stop Oil will be stepping up day after day, causing disruption and putting their liberty on the line to demand that the government ends new oil and gas.”
Ben-Julian Harrington, chief constable of Essex, said: “It is a really dangerous and difficult environment. I think they’re crazy.”
The force said its priority was “to keep our county moving”, but added that it had closed the bridge because of its duty of care to the protesters and those involved in any resolution.
The decision to stop traffic resulted in six miles of tailbacks on yesterday and today, including many freight vehicles. The Dartford Crossing is the only way to cross the Thames east of London by road.
The protest angered many in the local community. Footage posted online showed the protesters being targeted with fireworks on Monday night as they dangled from the bridge.
Today was the 18th successive day of Just Stop Oil protests. The group suggested that it had blocked the bridge because of the presence of several oil depots in the area.

Trowland said in a selfie video yesterday: “It is really difficult to hold on to this cable. I’m willing to do this kind of thing because I’m not ready to sit back and watch everything burn for the rest of my life. And that is what’s happening. We are going to stay here until the government makes a meaningful statement that they will end new licensing consent for oil and gas extraction of oil in the UK.”
On Friday two Just Stop Oil protesters threw tins of tomato soup at the £72.5 million Vincent van Gogh painting Sunflowers at the National Gallery in London.
The group has been served with an injunction to prevent what Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, described as “disruptive tactics”. Khan said that the injunction would give police further powers of arrest as well as enabling damages to be awarded if the order is breached.
“I’m someone who believes passionately we should be tackling climate change, but some of the tactics used by Just Stop Oil are causing massive disruption,” the mayor said. “It’s really important when people feel strongly about these things they should protest peacefully and it should be safe. It’s really important when people feel strongly about these things they should protest peacefully and it should be safe.”
Trowland said: “As a professional civil engineer, each year as I renew my registration I commit to acting within our code of ethics, which requires me to safeguard human life and welfare and the environment.Our government has enacted suicidal laws to accelerate oil production, killing human life and destroying our environment.
“I can’t challenge this madness in my desk job, designing bridges, so I’m taking direct action, occupying the QEII bridge until the government stops all new oil.”
Marcus said: “Only direct action will now help to reach the social tipping point we so urgently need.”
The Metropolitan Police are struggling to stop repeat offenders because prosecutors require a full case file, which should include statements and video evidence, before making a charging decision for offences such as obstruction of the highway.
Anna Holland, 20, of Newcastle upon Tyne, and Phoebe Plummer, 21, of Clapham, south London, appeared before Westminster magistrates’ court on Saturday and were charged with criminal damage to the frame of the Van Gogh painting. The painting itself was not damaged.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/britain.title: Britain’s secret rainforests — and how to spot them
https://www.thetimes.com/article/britain.text:
The weather is perfect. Misty, moody and atmospheric: this is how Dartmoor is meant to be. Months of city stresses are blown away as the breeze picks up, the endless sea of grass and gorse billowing as we hike uphill. A kestrel hovers overhead, searching for prey on the heath, constantly adjusting its wings to keep its body utterly motionless as the wind gusts around it.
Dartmoor has always fascinated people, drawing them in and repelling them in equal measures. Arthur Conan Doyle, speaking through Dr Watson in The Hound of the Baskervilles, described it as a “God-forsaken corner of the world”. But spending time here, Watson admitted, let the “spirit of the moor sink into one’s soul, its vastness, and also its grim charm. When you are once out upon its bosom you have left all traces of modern England behind you.”
I spent a summer here when I was a student, taking groups of holidaymakers walking on the hills. Half a lifetime ago, the otherworldliness of this bleak landscape left a deep impression. It is not the vast moor, however, that has brought me back — it is the promise of a secret treasure hidden within its folds.
Striding alongside me is the environmentalist Guy Shrubsole, 37. Tall and slim, wearing a battered old Barbour jacket and jeans above his walking boots, he bounds easily up a giant mound of granite known as Bench Tor. “That”, he beams, pointing down to the deep valley that has suddenly appeared below us, “is a rainforest.”
Rainforests, I had always thought, belong in the Tropics: the Amazon, the Congo, the islands of Borneo and Sumatra — those lush, wet jungles where towering trees are draped with vines and orchids, and countless species thrive.
But here, blanketing the steep valley wall all the way down to the River Dart rushing 500ft below, is a dripping, steaming woodland. Mist rises in plumes from the canopy of oak and ash. Jackets of moss clothe ancient bark; long beards of lichen and ferns hang from gnarled branches. We could be gazing at a scene from Conan Doyle’s The Lost World, or its modern equivalent, Jurassic Park.
This is a temperate rainforest. In the Tropics a rainforest is somewhere wet enough for the trees to have other plants growing on them. In cooler climes you look for similar clues. Epiphytes — plants that grow on other plants — are the key indicator.
There are not very many places on the planet where temperate rainforest can flourish. It has to be wet — with about 1,400mm of rain a year (London gets about 700mm). But it also has to be mild enough for plants to grow in mid-air, held aloft, high above the earth’s warm embrace. These are fragile ecosystems growing in small patches across the world: America’s Pacific Northwest, Chile’s southern tip, parts of Japan, Korea and New Zealand. But they truly thrive on the wet Atlantic fringe of the British Isles.
“Temperate rainforests are the very pinnacle of Britain’s woodlands,” Shrubsole writes in his new book, The Lost Rainforests of Britain. “They support about 500 species of lichen and more than 160 species of mosses and liverworts … When it comes to temperate rainforest, Britain is world-beating.”
At one time rainforest covered a fifth of the British landmass, a great strip of lush woodland stretching through Cornwall, Devon, Wales and the Lake District and up the west coast of Scotland. What ecologists call Britain’s “bioclimatic rainforest zone” — the area where it is warm and wet enough for rainforest — covers 11 million acres. Today, only isolated scraps of this once great sylvan wilderness survive. Combined, they cover about 330,000 acres or just 0.5 per cent of Britain.
The forest below us, labelled White Wood on the map, is one of these remaining scraps. It has clung on here since the last Ice Age, surviving for 10,000 years thanks to its remote position, steep sides and tough terrain. The valley is dotted with ankle-breaking boulder fields — a deterrent to loggers and sheep alike.
We find a path through the bracken and traverse at an angle down the slope, picking our way past rowan, dotted with scarlet berries, and blackthorn, heavy with sloes. Occasionally a lone birch tree sprouts through the scrub, a sign that the forest may be regenerating and expanding. “This is the advance party,” Shrubsole says. “Rowan and birch tend to be the early colonisers. Oak and ash lumber behind.”
We reach the tree line and enter the woods. Shrubsole compares the experience to entering a cathedral, the light filtering through “stained-glass windows of translucent leaves”. The atmosphere changes, like stepping out of a busy sun-drenched street into a dark church. Sounds are muffled — even the roar of the Dart seems quieter now. The Celtic druids considered these woodlands to be sacred. It is easy to see why.
Shrubsole is in his element here. He reels off the names of the mosses and ferns, counting 15 or 20 species growing on a single oak. He delights in pointing out strange lichens with eccentric names — string-of-sausage, rock tripe, witches’ whiskers, jam tart. He crouches over a moss-covered boulder and exclaims with delight, passing me a hand lens. “That is a filmy fern,” he says, as I peer at a mass of tiny translucent fronds, shimmering as they peek out from a blanket of moss. “They are just one cell thick. They are a good rainforest indicator because they only grow where it is constantly wet.”
A few yards later he points out a holly and a rowan that have each rooted halfway up the trunk of a single birch. A miniature forest, an entire aerial ecosystem, has established itself. “Life is piled up on top of other life,” he says. “That’s the way it is here.”
I ask if he has always been fascinated by plants, or whether he was interested in animals first. “I’ve always liked the minutiae of things,” he says. “I was obsessed with ants when I was a kid. But when it comes to plants, we just don’t see them. We know that if it’s green, it’s nice, but our brains don’t differentiate between them.”
This “plant-blindness” is a symptom of our separation from nature, he believes. Many people now cannot name our most common native trees by sight, let alone the mosses or lichens growing on their bark. This complacency is part of the reason few people know about Britain’s rainforests or grieve their loss. “This great forgetting that we once had rainforests is almost as heartbreaking as the loss of the forests themselves,” Shrubsole writes.
We continue our walk through White Wood, pausing to remark on the size of the huge red toadstools growing from the forest floor. We say hello to two elderly women walking a dog. They are the first people we have seen all day.
“Do you think they know this is a rainforest?” I ask when they have passed. “And does it matter?” Shrubsole thinks for a moment. “On one level, no,” he says. “They know it’s a lovely place. But on another level, it does matter. If people don’t know these rainforests exist, how will they know what they have lost? I hope to re-enchant people about these places. They give an insight into a different past but also a different future, in which we do more to protect what we have.”
And these woods are worth protecting, he insists. The trees themselves, but also the layers of moss and humus that form on the branches, are efficient stores of carbon, a useful tool in the battle against climate change.
Our temperate rainforests, like their tropical cousins, also harbour a huge wealth of flora and fauna. A 2018 report by the Joint Nature Conservation Committee said the UK has an “international responsibility” to protect its rainforests as vital habitats.
Shrubsole argues that our temperate rainforests are worth preserving for their own sake. “We have to get back to a less instrumental idea of the environment. It has a right to exist and we shouldn’t be ashamed of framing it that way.” He points to British hand-wringing about the state of rainforests overseas. “There is an element of hypocrisy about this,” he says. This weekend environmentalists are nervously watching the results of the Brazilian election, for fear that Jair Bolsonaro — accused of trashing the Amazon — is re-elected. “We tell Brazil to protect its rainforests but we do nothing to bring back our own,” Shrubsole says.
His book is only a part of his mission. Over the past two years he has been trying to map the scraps of temperate rainforests that cling on in modern Britain. If we don’t know where these remaining fragments are, we cannot protect them. Yet until now no definitive map exists.
Using his blog and Twitter, he has urged the public to send in photos of potential sites and has driven thousands of miles around the country visiting and verifying the finds. He has been inundated with responses all the way up the west coast. To his surprise, he has also been alerted to many sites outside what was considered to be the west coast rainforest zone. He even received reports of patches of forest hundreds of miles away in the gullies and ghylls of the Weald, in the relatively dry counties of Kent, Sussex and Surrey. Ecologists now believe rainforests can grow in damp microclimates outside their normal zone.
“This raises an exciting possibility,” Shrubsole writes. “By allowing woodland cover to regenerate, could we actually see an expansion of the temperate rainforest zone?” Planting trees — which itself creates a damp microclimate — may eventually result in the right conditions for more rainforests.
If anyone was born to save Britain’s rainforests, it was Guy Shrubsole. His parents, James and Lorna, set up the Newbury branch of Friends of the Earth in the 1970s. “They were middle-class environmentalists,” he says. “I was very much influenced by their values and upbringing.”
In 1996, at the age of ten, he marched against the Newbury bypass. “At the time it was the biggest environmental protest Britain had ever seen — there were 8,000 people on that march and we walked the route of the bypass from one end to the other. I went back again with Mum and Dad after they cut down the trees — I distinctly remember Mum saying it reminded her of the pictures of the Amazon being cut down.”
He attended the local comprehensive school where his parents were teachers. A keen cross-country runner, he got his first glimpse of Dartmoor as he ran the infamous Ten Tors, a 45-mile race for teenagers organised by the British Army.
Shrubsole went on to study history at Oxford before becoming a civil servant in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, investigating the impact of climate on the food chain. A similar job followed for the New Zealand government. He later worked as an environmental campaigner for Friends of the Earth and Rewilding Britain. But it was writing that made Shrubsole’s name. His first book, Who Owns England?, published in 2019, was an instant Sunday Times bestseller.
Two years ago, between lockdowns, Shrubsole and his girlfriend, Louisa Casson, 31, an oceans campaigner at Greenpeace, moved from London to Devon. Exploring Dartmoor from his new home near Totnes, he discovered Britain’s rainforests — and set out to save them.
It is raining now, and Shrubsole and I quicken our pace as we near the car park high on the moor. We shelter in his car, a six-year-old Vauxhall Viva nicknamed Zoomer in ironic reference to its performance on the Devon hills. Examining the map as the rain comes down, Shrubsole points out the local landmarks — Birch Tor, Thornworthy Down, Hawthorn Clitter. Most of Dartmoor, he says, used to be covered in rainforest — the names on the map give a clue to the ghost woods that haunt this barren landscape.
“It is a massive, wet desert,” he says as we drive across the moor. “You might think it’s wild and unspoilt, but it has been changed by humanity.” The bleak moor that I and so many others love, it turns out, is nothing more than a barren monoculture of grass.
He points out patches of brighter green in the distance, squared off by stone walls. “Those fields have been ploughed and replanted with rye grass for better pasture,” he says. “It is completely artificial.” This transformation isn’t a modern phenomenon. It started in the Stone Age, when hunter-gatherers began to work the land, clearing the forest with flint axes. But it was sheep farming, introduced by monks in the Middle Ages, that proved to be the nail in the coffin for Britain’s woodland. From Dartmoor to the Yorkshire Dales, forests disappeared as sheep advanced.
The problem, Shrubsole says, is that sheep do not allow forests to regenerate. As soon as any new sapling emerges from the soil, it is nibbled away. And unlike cattle, many breeds of sheep farmed in the UK stay on the hill year-round, giving the landscape no time to recover.
Some environmentalists have all but gone to war over the issue. Shrubsole takes a slightly gentler approach, but he believes a big part of the problem is the idea that criticising sheep somehow represents an attack on British tradition. “The thing I hate is the idea of a cultural landscape,” he says. “You get it particularly in the Lake District, which is seen as the ‘republic of shepherds’, the perfect union between man and nature. But which era’s culture are we defending? Which history are we talking about preserving? There is nothing natural about it. There are twice as many sheep in the Lake District today as there were in the 1950s.”
He insists he is not advocating wall-to-wall rainforest, even if it were possible. The bogs and mires that cover parts of Dartmoor are also an invaluable carbon sink and a vital habitat: sphagnum mosses, birds and amphibians have made their home on the peat formed when the remains of old rainforests sunk into the ground. Draining these bogs to plant forests would be environmental vandalism. His vision is for a “mosaic” of farmland and wildflower meadow, interspersed with peat bog and woodland. That would help farmers, he says, providing shade for animals in the summer and helping to alleviate the drought conditions we have seen in recent years.
“Let’s start with rainforest restoration, because I think it captures people’s imagination as well as providing an incredibly rich ecosystem,” he says. “You start by allowing it to regenerate where it naturally goes. It follows the valleys, the boulder fields and the steep-sided hillsides. These are not areas that are productive farmland anyway.”
He has spent the past few months attempting to build consensus on Dartmoor, encouraging networks of like-minded farmers, landowners and conservation bodies to try to regenerate and expand the rainforests that exist. Such groups have already started springing up.
If grazing were prevented on the edge of existing rainforests, creating “buffer zones” of just 150 metres on all sides, Shrubsole calculates the area of temperate rainforest across Britain could double. Of course it would take time but as we saw at the edge of White Wood, forests are constantly trying to expand. Nature finds a way.
We get out of Zoomer and set out to another rainforest, Wistman’s Wood. A mile and a half up the hill, it becomes visible across the heath, a dark brooding patch in a dip in the fell. While White Wood seemed perfectly at home in its wet valley, Wistman’s is incongruous, an eight-acre scrap of woodland in the middle of an otherwise barren landscape. It has become so popular among the Instagram generation that Natural England has asked people not to enter the heart of the forest.
We step just inside the wood and already it is like nature on steroids. The trees here are even more bent and gnarled than the ones we have already seen, and they host even more species. One tree has an entire bilberry bush growing from its bark, along with woodrush, mosses and lichens. “It’s like an ancient sea monster unfurling from the rock,” Shrubsole says.
All these trees are ancient — there are no saplings, even on the forest fringe. Acorns hang from the branches and litter the floor but among them we see sheep droppings. If an acorn does take seed, it doesn’t stand a chance. Shrubsole has tried several times to persuade the Duchy of Cornwall, which owns this land, to fence around the wood to allow it to regenerate and expand. He has had no luck so far, but hopes Prince William, the new Duke of Cornwall, might be more amenable than his father was.
Wistman’s Wood has been associated with myth and legend for generations. The name derives from the Devonshire “wisht”, meaning eerie or uncanny. According to local folklore, it was a sacred grove where Celtic druids gave sacrifice to the gods. It is also known as the home of the “wisht hounds” — the phantom dogs that ran alongside the Wild Hunt, a supernatural chase across the moor led by the Devil. Shrubsole is convinced this was the inspiration for Conan Doyle’s Baskerville hound.
He believes Britain’s rainforests are woven into much of our culture and ancient stories. We have just forgotten them. The Mabinogion is a collection of Welsh myths that was first written down about 1,000 years ago, but their oral tradition dates back much further. The name of the central character, the wizard Gwydion, can be translated as “wood-wise”. The term “druid” means “oak-seer”. Even “Gaelic” is derived from a word meaning “forest people”. From Shakespeare’s Birnam Wood, advancing on Dunsinane in Macbeth, to Tolkien’s march of the Ents, the idea of the woodland as a supernatural protective force is entwined in our culture.
“Doing something to repair the damage done to our own rainforests here in Britain — ‘this other Eden’, this ‘green and pleasant land’, as our greatest playwrights and poets would have it — feels like a redemptive quest,” Shrubsole writes. “In restoring them, we might yet restore a missing part of ourselves.”
The Lost Rainforests of Britain by Guy Shrubsole is published by William Collins at £20
Epiphytes — plants that grow on other plants — are a big clue. The key is abundance. Anywhere wet enough to host a mass of lichens, mosses and fungi is a likely candidate.
Beefsteak fungus (Fistulina hepatica) resembles a slab of raw meat — complete with dripping blood. It thrives on oaks in both dry woodlands and rainforests.
Octopus suckers (Collema fasciculare) could have crawled out of a B-movie, but are a type of jelly lichen found in the rainforests of western Scotland.
Hazel gloves fungus (Hypocreopsis rhododendri) is found only on decaying branches of rare hazelwoods on the Atlantic coast.
Lobaria virens, a green, shiny lichen marked by orange disks, thrives in the dampest parts of the Lake District, Wales, Scotland and the West Country.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/liz-tru.title: These are tough times — Britain needs us to step up, says Liz Truss
https://www.thetimes.com/article/liz-tru.text:
Britain is too reluctant to “do things differently”, Liz Truss declared, as she attacked the “enemies of enterprise” and staked her premiership on boosting growth through disruptive reforms.
In a combative 34-minute speech at the end of a tumultuous Conservative party conference in Birmingham, the prime minister pledged to face down critics who have attacked her tax- cutting agenda.
She said that lowering taxes was “the right thing to do morally and economically” but admitted that she had been wrong to prioritise scrapping the 45p rate. “I get it and I have listened,” she told party members.
Truss said that her economic policies were the only way Britain could break a “high-tax, low-growth cycle” and spread prosperity. “I have three priorities for our economy: growth, growth, and growth,” she said as she promised to demolish barriers to business.
Truss opened by describing the situation facing Britain as a “tempest” for which she blamed Covid and Russia. “These are stormy days,” she said. “Together, we have mourned the death of Queen Elizabeth II, the rock on which modern Britain was built. We are now in a new era under King Charles III.
“We are dealing with the global economic crisis caused by Covid and by Putin’s appalling war in Ukraine. In these tough times, we need to step up. I am determined to get Britain moving, to get us through the tempest and put us on a stronger footing as a nation.”
That was the first of three times when the prime minister referred to the “global economic crisis”, as she tried to deflect blame for surging interest rates from the market reaction to her budget.
Truss acknowledged the turmoil of her first month in office but argued it was a part of breaking a “high-tax, low-growth cycle”. Arguing for far-reaching economic change and the need to “do things differently”, she said: “As the last few weeks have shown, it will be difficult. Wherever there is change, there is disruption, and not everybody will be in favour of change, but everyone will benefit from the result.”
She drew on her childhood in Paisley and Leeds to argue that boosting growth benefited everyone. “I’ve seen the boarded-up shops, I’ve seen people left with no hope turning to drugs, I’ve seen families struggling to put food on the table,” she said.
The prime minister praised Kwasi Kwarteng as her “dynamic new chancellor” and said cutting taxes was justified “morally and economically”.
Just after Truss said that she was not willing to “consign our great country to decline”, two Greenpeace protesters stood up with a banner demanding to know “who voted for this?”. Truss said “let’s get them removed” before quipping that they had begun their protest too soon as she would be assailing people like them later in the speech.
Truss cast her opponents as the “anti-growth coalition”, determined to “hold us back”. The group, she said, included: “Labour, the Lib Dems and the SNP, the militant unions, the vested interests dressed up as think tanks, the talking heads, the Brexit deniers and Extinction Rebellion and some of the people we had in the hall earlier.”
• David Aaronovitch: Trussonomics leaves Labour in a hole• The Times view on the Conservative leader’s next steps: Truss’s Task
Truss, who has lived for many years in southeast London, continued: “They taxi from north London townhouses to the BBC studio to dismiss anyone challenging the status quo. From broadcast to podcast, they peddle the same old answers. It’s always more taxes, more regulation and more meddling.”
In contrast, Truss said she was on the side of the “white van drivers, the hairdressers, the plumbers, the accountants, the IT workers and millions of others.”
“I love enterprise,” Truss said. “I love that people can take responsibility, start a business and invest. They generate profit, they give new jobs, they power new growth. That is why we’re backing business to the hilt.” She said that plans to create investment zones with lower levels of tax and regulation would “harness the power of free enterprise”. She vowed to “keep an iron grip” on public finances and said she was committed to “sound money”.
In an unusually personal section, Truss described how her politics had been motivated by sexism she had faced. Recalling how she was given a junior air hostess badge while her brothers got junior pilot badges, she said: “It wasn’t the only time in my life that I’d been treated differently for being female or for not fitting in. It made me angry. And it made me determined to change things.” Describing herself as the first prime minister educated at a comprehensive, Truss reiterated her criticism of her school in Leeds. “I saw too many children being let down, let down by low expectations, let down by a Labour council who were more interested in political correctness than they were in school standards,” she said.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
MondayMy friends, it’s great to be here with you in Birmingham. It’s fantastic to see the cranes across the skyline, the busy trams coursing down the streets, and Kwasi Kwarteng standing here in my hotel room, hyperventilating into a paper bag.
“Look,” he says eventually. “Whose fault is it? The 45p thing? Because I’m about to do the U-turn. And I’m still not sure who we blame.”
Difficult. But important. Blaming people is a central part of what we do.
“It was a collective decision,” says Chris Philp, who is the chief secretary to the Treasury. “Blame is pointless.”
“I suppose we could blame Chris,” says Kwasi.
“Wait, what?” says Chris.
“What about Vladimir Putin?” suggests Nadhim Zahawi.
“This is ridiculous,” says Ben Wallace. “You’ll be blaming the Queen next.”
“Hey wow,” says Kwasi. “Good call.”
TuesdayPlanning my own speech now. The whole gang has come for afternoon tea. And we agree we need to grow the pie.
“Don’t blame me,” says Thérèse Coffey, guiltily. “It was already quite small when I got here.”
“Just remember the hall is on your side,” says Jacob Rees-Mogg.
“Especially the empty chairs,” says Kemi Badenoch.
“For too long,” I say, “our economy has not grown as it should have done.”
“Maybe don’t say precisely how long, though,” suggests Tom Tugendhat.
“I’ve seen despair,” I say. “I’ve seen people with no hope turning to drugs.”
“Same,” says Penny. “In a fringe meeting last night.”
“Share your dreams!” says Suella Braverman. “My dream is that a flight will take asylum seekers to Rwanda!”
“My dreams aren’t great at the moment,” says Kwasi, distantly.
“Mine are usually about Margaret Thatcher,” says Jacob.
“I really want to exceed expectations,” I say, scribbling all of this down.
“That,” says Kemi, “won’t be hard.”
WednesdaySpeech written! Now I’m practising. I’ve just got to the bit about knowing how it feels to be underestimated, because I once got given a “Junior Air Hostess” badge while my brothers got “Junior Pilots”.
“And nobody,” I continue, “wants to live in a country where eight-year-old girls aren’t allowed to fly planes!”
But weirdly, everybody says I should take that out.
I’m also not sure I’ve listed enough enemies we can blame for everything that goes wrong. Especially as Jacob wants me to ditch “vested interests” because his nanny won’t let him leave the house if he isn’t wearing one.
“Labour!” I say. “The Lib Dems, the SNP, Brexit deniers, Extinction Rebellion, and people who live in north London townhouses! Who am I forgetting?”
“North London is awfully specific,” says Kwasi.
“Maybe it should be anyone who lives in a house anywhere?” suggests Suella.
“And what about,” I say, “the talking heads and defenders of the status quo?”
“Bit random,” says Nadhim. “Some 90s bands were far worse.”
ThursdaySpeech done, conference over. Now I’ve flown to a European summit in Prague. I’m particularly keen to speak to Emmanuel Macron about what he can do to discourage migrants from coming to Britain.
“Entre nous,” he says, “I doubt I can discourage them as much as you have in the past fortnight.”
I tell him that my home secretary dreams of planes taking asylum seekers to Rwanda. And he says his dreams are much more exciting than that.
“Mais,” he adds, “I do eat a lot of cheese.”
“Now you’re just showing off,” I say.
FridayThérèse, who is the deputy PM, says that while I was away the National Grid warned of electricity shortages. Apparently people are quite worried about it. Especially as I just overruled a plan for rationing.
“The point is,” I say, summoning Jacob, who is my energy secretary, “we don’t believe in telling people what to do!”
“Is this about Chocolate Oranges?” asks Jacob, because he’s been having a fight about those, too.
“It’s the same!” I say. “It’s one long war against the anti-growth coalition!”
Jacob agrees. Although he is still worried, he says, about who we’ll blame if we do run out.
“We’ll find someone,” I say.
“Don’t look at me,” says Thérèse. “I don’t even like them.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/tofu-re.title: Tofu recipes fit for the ‘wokerati’: a beginner’s guide
https://www.thetimes.com/article/tofu-re.text:
Suella Braverman probably thought she was being funny when she coined the term “tofu-eating wokerati” yesterday. Speaking in the House of Commons, the then home secretary blamed the recent disruptions caused by the eco-protest group Just Stop Oil on the “anti-growth coalition”, made up of the Labour Party, the Lib Dems and said tofu eaters.
The thing is, being called a tofu muncher these days isn’t actually an insult. Rather it’s a confirmation that you are culinarily in vogue. Tofu is cool; Braverman had admitted she was not. A day later, she was toast. Robert Peston tweeted that she had been asked to resign “over an issue relating to ‘security’ ” — but perhaps her disparaging remark about bean curd was really to blame. Was it just a coincidence that the chancellor, Jeremy Hunt, had been compared to a tofu burger the same day?
In 2020 sales of tofu in Britain rose by 82 per cent and it has remained popular. You are probably sitting in the same room as a tofu eater now. Last month Waitrose extended its ready-meal range to include several tofu dishes, from sweet and sour to a stir-fry.● Suella Braverman departs as home secretary, plunging Truss into new crisis
It’s one of the most in-demand dishes at Bubala, the critics’ favourite vegetarian restaurant in Soho, London, where it’s served with harissa — a foodie’s store cupboard essential. Wild by Tart, the upmarket restaurant in Belgravia, London, has published numerous recipes on how to cook it. Wild by Tart, incidentally, is co-owned by Jemima Jones, wife of the financier Ben Goldsmith, not Braverman’s idea of a typical tofu muncher.
For those eager to join in, there are a few things you need to know. Tofu is made from soya beans. There are two types: Japanese silken tofu, which has a custard-like texture, and regular Chinese tofu, which is firm and pressed into blocks. Silken tofu can work as a dairy alternative in creamy foods such as dressings, sauces and dips. Regular tofu can be sliced and treated more like a meat substitute, diced and baked, fried or deep-fried.
Before cooking Chinese tofu, you will need to drain it to get rid of excess water. Wrap the block in a tea towel and put a wooden chopping board on top, weighted with something heavy. Let it drain for 20 minutes until it’s firmed up.As for the taste, vegans will describe it as bean-y, but as a meat-lover I see it more as a vehicle for flavour. Which is why you need to hit firm tofu with big flavours — chilli, honey, ginger, soya, paprika.
To cook tofu, either drain it, marinate then fry, or do as the chef Yotam Ottolenghi and fry it in hot oil, dusted in a bit of cornflour for crisp, and add the flavours after. I prefer the latter because I’ve never found tofu to be as sponge-like as some chefs say.If you’re going to stir-fry it, it’s easier to cook it separately then add it to the vegetables at the last minute so it stays crisp. Other chefs, such as Bonnie Chung, who wrote the recipe book Tofu Tasty, like to mash their tofu. She says: “Mashed tofu entwines with other ingredients. You’ll need to make sure it’s properly drained so you don’t serve it with excess water.”● Marina O’Loughlin reviews Bubala restaurant in London
Ingredients800g firm tofu, cubed and tossed in cornflour150g butter12 small shallots, thinly sliced8 red chillies, thinly sliced12 garlic cloves, crushed3 tbsp chopped fresh root ginger3 tbsp sweet soy sauce3 tbsp light soy sauce4 tsp dark soy sauce2 tbsp caster sugar5 tbsp crushed black peppercorns1 bunch of spring onions, sliced
MethodFry the tofu in vegetable oil until golden all over and have a thin crust. Remove from the pan. In a new pan on a low to medium heat, melt the butter. Add the shallots, chillies, garlic and ginger. Sauté for 15 min until the ingredients are shiny and totally soft. Add the soy sauces and sugar and stir, then the pepper. Add the tofu to warm it up then stir in the onions and serve with hot rice. ottolenghi.co.uk/recipes
Ingredients2 x 280g tofu blocks, drained, sliced into rectangles and dusted in cornflour1 garlic clove, peeled and grated4 tbsp maple syrup2 tbsp harissa paste1 tbsp tomato puree1 tsp white wine vinegar200g vegan natural yoghurtSmall handful of fresh coriander, choppedJuice of half a lime
MethodFry the tofu in vegetable oil for 10 min until golden. Remove from the pan. Fry the garlic. Add the maple syrup, harissa, tomato puree, vinegar and stir until saucy. In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt, coriander and lime for your dipping sauce. Garnish the crispy tofu with sesame seeds and serve together.For hundreds of vegan recipes visit bosh.tv and follow @bosh.tv on Instagram.
Ingredients1 x 300g tofu block, drained and crumbled1 red onion, finely sliced1 small pepper, sliced2 garlic cloves, grated2 tbsp unsalted butter1 tsp Dijon mustard1 tbsp nutritional yeast flakes1 tsp turmeric1½ tsp paprika35g plain flourHandful baby spinachCoriander, roughly chopped
MethodFry the onion, red pepper and garlic for 3 to 4 min until softened. Add the butter and mustard and stir. Then add the tofu and remove from the heat. Mix the yeast, turmeric, paprika, flour and salt then add to the saucepan with the soya milk in. Keep stirring until smooth. Pour the sauce over the tofu and stir. Add the chilli flakes and spinach. Serve on toast with coriander.From Tofu Tasty: Imaginative Tofu Recipes For Every Day by Bonnie Chung

https://www.thetimes.com/article/hallowe.title: Halloween costumes — will you be a lettuce or Taylor Swift tonight?
https://www.thetimes.com/article/hallowe.text:
Boo!Nothing scares me any more — 2022 is the year I developed unprecedented resolve.
Really? Not even Dahmer?Oh no. That I had to turn off after the first episode. I dread to think how many people dressed up as him over the weekend. Come to think of it, do you think some cannibalistic trick or treaters might rock up at my door tonight in blond wigs and glasses?
You know what, I doubt it.Why?
Because there are so, so many better costume options this Halloween. Like what?
Where to begin? It’s an embarrassment of riches! But with Liz Truss, I think. Actually, no — the lettuce that outlasted Liz Truss, which is probably now a more ghoulish, gruesome (but no less smug) green. I love it. More!
You could go as the mini-budget (terrifying). Or, even scarier, “the markets”.Ooooh, spooky! What will they do next?!
Speaking of, perhaps just come as an energy bill — or your new mortgage rate. Or, for a fuzzier political option, Larry the cat. Cute, yet timely. What else?
I am very much hoping to see people dress up as copies of Spare, Prince Harry’s upcoming memoir. Perhaps everyone should just dress as their “authentic selves”.
I can’t think of anything worse. Better to dress as Taylor Swift’s chaotic alter ego from her new music video for Anti-Hero — it has had 37 million views and counting in one week.Obviously it does, the song is a banger.
What about going to a party as a Just Stop Oil protester? Glue yourself to the dancefloor! Or one of the artworks they have defaced — cover yourself in soup.Good one!
Here’s a few more ideas: a dragon from House of the Dragon; Donald Trump; Putin; a Stranger Things cast member; the Harry Styles/Florence Pugh/Olivia Wilde love triangle; Bennifer; Pamela Anderson.I feel as if I am about to witness the year in review — 2022, what a horror show.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Bob Geldof: I don’t like criticism of so-called white saviours
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
When Stacey Dooley was filmed hugging a Ugandan toddler on a filming trip with Comic Relief, it led to a backlash against “white saviours”, who were accused of spreading stereotypes from the colonial era.
Now the most celebrated white saviour of modern times, Bob Geldof, has hit back at such criticism, calling it “trite and silly”.
Geldof, who created the Live Aid concert that helped to raise £150 million for famine relief, told Radio Times: “Black saviours, white saviours, green saviours, I’m with them all.”
Geldof was inspired to write the Band Aid charity hit Do They Know It’s Christmas? after watching a report on the 1984 Ethiopian famine by Michael Buerk on the BBC’s Six O’Clock News. The following year he put on the benefit concert at Wembley stadium, echoed by a similar concert in Philadelphia.
Despite being reluctant to talk about the events of 38 years ago, he has given an interview to Alan Yentob, which is being screened next week on BBC4.
Other fundraising efforts followed in his wake, but in 2019 there was controversy after Dooley, a celebrity ambassador for Comic Relief, was filmed hugging a photogenic Ugandan toddler.
The Labour MP David Lammy tweeted that “the world doesn’t need any more white saviours”, and The Guardian, in a clear reference to Geldof, said that “white saviours belong in the 1980s”.
Comic Relief later said its appeals for Red Nose Day would be led by local film-makers for a “more authentic perspective”. Sir Lenny Henry, co-founder of Comic Relief, said: “African people don’t want us to tell their stories for them. What they need is more agency, a platform and partnership.”
Following the row, Comic Relief suffered an £8 million fall in donations for its Red Nose Day appeal, compared with its previous appeal in 2017.
Asked if charities now try too hard to steer clear of such criticism, Geldof told Radio Times: “I don’t think most people give a f*** about that. It’s just a wormhole that people have disappeared down, where everything can be deconstructed.
“But it’s trite and silly, in my view. If someone is hurt and I personally see it, and I’m aware of it, I’ll do what I can to make them less hurt.”
Geldof, who was given an honorary knighthood in 1986, admitted that the Band Aid hit, which has sold more than three million copies in the UK and raised more than £200 million, drives him “mad” when it is played at Christmas. He said: “The song has a life of its own. It raises money every time it’s played in every f***ing supermarket. It’s Mistletoe and Wine at vegetables, Slade at baked beans, Wizzard for tea and coffee and Band Aid at the butcher’s counter. It drives me f***ing mad at Christmas. But there it is.”
He also voiced his support for the climate change protesters who threw tomato soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers at the National Gallery in London as part of a campaign of “continuous disruption” by Just Stop Oil. Phoebe Plummer, 21, and Anna Holland, 20, were bailed by Westminster magistrates after pleading not guilty to criminal damage charges.
Geldof said: “The climate activists are 1,000 per cent right. And 1,000 per cent I support them. It’s offensive to destroy Van Gogh’s genius. That achieves nothing. But it was clever to throw it on the glass knowing it wouldn’t be destroyed. That’s just annoying. And annoying is quite good.
“I was driving to Hyde Park when the Extinction Rebellion people blocked it and I was f***ing furious. But I wasn’t railing against them. I was thinking, ‘If I was 18, would I be there?’ and the answer is yes.
“Annoying people into policy change may not work. Does that mean I’m against their passion? Their anger? Their bravery? No. Would I put up with it? They’re not killing anyone. Climate change will.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/as-the-.title: As the cost of heating soars, MPs and peers ‘swelter at 30C’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/as-the-.text:
Rooms in parliament are said to be heated to 30C despite the soaring price of gas and electricity.
MPs have complained of overheating inside the poorly insulated Palace of Westminster and have demanded that the government improves energy use. They say some offices and meeting rooms in the “leaky” building are either freezing cold or unbearably hot.
Temperature readings taken by The Times with a thermal imaging camera showed heat escaping through open windows. Measurements taken outside the House of Lords recorded temperatures in rooms of 23C, 26C and 30C.
The rooms, understood to be offices and meeting spaces, overlook Old Palace Yard above the Peers’ Entrance on the West Front of the building.
Guy Opperman, a minister for work and welfare, said that some rooms in parliament are heated to 30 degrees. During the Energy Prices Bill committee stage in the Commons he said: “In Germany and France they do not heat their buildings more than 19 degrees.”
He said some rooms seem to have the heating on full blast. “For example, there are certain rooms in the House of Lords, there are certain rooms certainly in Portcullis House [where MPs’ offices are], and genuinely people have windows open even in the height of winter, which is insane.”
Individual politicians have little control over the temperature in rooms, which are regulated centrally.
The Green MP Caroline Lucas said: “I appreciate it’s an old building, but nonetheless it is absolutely ridiculous that we haven’t upgraded the heating system in parliament. I’ve been in rooms where it’s either absolutely baking and you cannot turn the radiators down, or conversely it’s absolutely freezing and there’s no heating at all.”
The Labour MP Clive Lewis said: “We’ve got the fans on at the moment because it’s too hot.”
Both MPs led a protest outside the House of Lords on one of the days when readings were taken, joined by a coalition of activists from Just Stop Oil, Insulate Britain, Extinction Rebellion and Energy For All.
Lucas demanded “free energy for those who can’t afford it” and also called for “those big energy companies [to] bloody well cough up and make sure that the poorest in society are not paying the highest price for a crisis that is none of their making”. Afterwards she said that “parliament ought to be a beacon of best practice, showing the way”, adding: “If we’re talking about spending millions on renovating parliament, we should first and foremost be making sure that the way that we heat our buildings is absolutely paramount.”
The Times took temperature measurements on separate days two weeks ago, in the morning and at night.
The House of Lords disputed the measurements, claiming that the central heating systems are not capable of reaching those temperatures. A spokesman said it is “simply untrue” that the rooms were “centrally heated” to those temperatures. It was suggested that some rooms could appear to have higher temperatures because of special equipment inside, such as dehumidifiers used to dry rooms affected by water ingress. However, a thermal-imaging specialist suggested that dehumidifiers would not be able to heat rooms to the temperatures that were measured and said radiators were the more likely cause.
The expert reviewed the readings and said that although he could not be certain about the procedure or what was inside the rooms, the images indicated a “waste of heat”.
Based on the footage he said: “What it shows in my opinion is that the room is hot or they are firing the heating out. It would suggest that the building performs poorly and they rely on excess heating to make it hot.”
Energy prices have been dramatically increasing around the world since Russia invaded Ukraine, which has disrupted production and exports and is contributing to the developing cost of living crisis in Britain.
Karen Wilding, 58, a climate activist, was shocked to hear that temperatures were so high in parliament and said it was “symptomatic of the problem” with Britain’s heating consumption.
“Who needs 30 degrees? What is that about? At home for me I’m on 16 degrees max,” she said. “Yeah, you have to put a jumper on, you have to put some socks on, what’s wrong with that?”
According to the House of Commons, when rooms have temperature controls for the user in parliament, there is a small threshold at which the temperature can be raised or lowered to ensure rooms are not over-cooled or overheated.
Parliament follows the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers’ guidelines for temperature standards in offices to ensure a comfortable working environment.
The building management system was upgraded recently to enable better control of the building, including the resetting of manual temperature changes each night to industry-recommended set points.
A spokesman for the House of Commons said: “Parliamentary authorities take energy efficiency very seriously and have a commitment to reducing parliament’s environmental impacts. Parliament operates to a pre-agreed heating season, which is modified annually according to weather conditions. This reflects the difficulties in overcoming thermal mass in a building with many difficult-to-heat spaces, and with considerable floor to ceiling heights and issues regarding the fabric of the building. As of September 2022, parliament has reduced gas consumption by 25 per cent since 2008-09.”
A spokesman for the House of Lords said: “We do not accept that the rooms were heated to the temperatures you are suggesting. It is simply untrue that the rooms have been centrally heated to those temperatures. The Palace of Westminster’s heating systems are not capable of reaching them.”
Opperman rejected their statements, saying: “No. They’re completely wrong. The facts are against them.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil bankrolled by fossil fuel heiress whose cash pays activists to protest
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
The Just Stop Oil activists who spent two nights last week suspended in hammocks above the Dartford Crossing in Kent were a long way from the main source of the group’s income: a coalition of wealthy individuals in the Hollywood Hills, including the heiress Aileen Getty.
Getty, 65, is the granddaughter of the oil tycoon J Paul Getty, once the richest man in the world. The family is thought to be worth £3.9 billion.
In 2020 she set up a non-profit organisation, the Climate Emergency Fund (CEF), which takes up the “bulk” of her time and resources. It distributes money to environmental campaign groups that use civil resistance in an attempt to effect change.
She has personally given more than £900,000, alongside other wealthy backers, including the Academy Award-winning film director Adam McKay and Rory Kennedy, a daughter of the assassinated senator Robert Kennedy.
This year the CEF gave its biggest grant — nearly £1 million — to Just Stop Oil. However, Just Stop Oil is not registered as a company or a charity in the UK, meaning the location and use of its wealth is not publicly declared. The millions of pounds of donations transferred to the campaign group goes to an unknown person’s bank account.
From her home in California, Getty follows the protests unfolding around the world. “It’s true that over a century ago, my family played a role in unlocking fossil fuels at a time when we did not know what we know now: that the extraction and use of fossil fuels is killing life on our planet,” she said.
In the past week Just Stop Oil has blocked roads, sprayed paint on Scotland Yard and Harrods, and splattered soup over Vincent van Gogh’s Sunflowers — protected by a glass screen — in the National Gallery in London.
“Disruptive climate activism is, I would argue, the single most underfunded area in philanthropy and a tremendous opportunity,” Getty, who has had both a charmed and troubled life, said. She is a recovering addict living with Aids, and an artist and activist. “We are out of time for anything other than rapid, comprehensive climate action.”
The CEF, of which Getty is a board member, has handed out more than £3.5 million to global climate organisations that use methods of mass civil resistance. A large proportion of its money goes to the “A22 Network” — a global coalition founded by the British organisations Just Stop Oil and Insulate Britain.
Insulate Britain, set up in September last year, demands that the government improve the insulation of all social housing in the UK by 2025; Just Stop Oil, founded in February, wants the UK government to halt all future licensing for the exploration, development and production of fossil fuels.
Today the network is made up of 12 groups in countries including Italy, New Zealand and Norway. To qualify, groups must be creating “public disruption” and asking for specific policy changes.
The two British groups have created the international blueprint for rebellion: in Germany protesters have glued themselves to roads; a woman in France cable-tied herself by the neck to a tennis net at the French Open; Italian activists glued themselves to the glass protecting Sandro Botticelli’s Primavera in Florence.
Getty gives money to the CEF, which in turn donates to climate activists — she does not have control over their specific actions and only funds legal activities.
Liam Norton, a spokesman for Insulate Britain, said that millions of pounds were divided between the A22 groups by “a coalition”, although it could not give names, spent on “the logistics of operations”. He said: “It’s also important for people to receive an income so they’re able to put these talks on.”
A spokesman for Just Stop Oil confirmed that “some people supporting Just Stop Oil do receive a small income”.
Online, Insulate Britain is no longer taking donations from members of the public. Just Stop Oil, however, has a crowdfunding page: it says £50 could pay for a young person to travel to an event; £100 could buy banners; £500 could hire a venue for a talk and cover leafleting costs; and £1,000 could pay for a Just Stop Oil team’s accommodation for a week. It has raised over £95,000. One of its Crowdfunder.com pages was closed by the website’s compliance team, as it did not cohere to its “terms of use”.
On the Just Stop Oil website, people can donate in the cryptocurrency Ethereum, which means that transactions are anonymous.
However, neither Just Stop Oil, Insulate Britain nor the A22 coalition is registered as a charity in the UK. They are therefore not required to show that the funds have been properly managed and used in line with the terms of the appeal.
By comparison, Extinction Rebellion defined itself as a “movement”, which received “practical support” from a registered private company, Compassionate Revolution. It declared a total income of £1.25 million last year.
The A22 group does not function in the same way. A spokesman said: “Just Stop Oil utilises a bank account held by supporters.”
For Getty, civil disobedience is the only option. “Instead of criticising young activists for trying to wake us up to the reality of our planet’s climate crisis,” she said, “we should ask ourselves how to be better partners to those who are inheriting our wreckage.”
The CEF said that Getty had never been personally involved in the fossil fuel trade. Getty Oil was founded by J Paul Getty in 1942 and the family sold Getty Oil in 1984.
She was brought up in Rome where, in 1973, her 16-year-old brother John Paul Getty III was held hostage for a ransom of £15 million. The money was paid by the patriarch only five months later and after his grandson’s ear was cut off by his captors and sent to a newspaper.
“A lot of the terror I witnessed as a young child and adult coloured my thoughts and art. I wasn’t protected like a lot of my relatives,” Getty said in 1990.
She survived drug addiction, a number of overdoses, anorexia, depression and self-harm. She married and later divorced Christopher Edward Wilding, the son of Elizabeth Taylor, who Getty called “Mom”. “Aileen is magic, what a survivor,” Taylor said before her death in 2011. “Her spirit is keeping her alive.”
In 1986 Getty was diagnosed with HIV and shortly after, Aids, contracted from a sexual partner. She turned her attention to activism. “I spend as much of my time as possible in nature, increasingly with a feeling of dread that as we continue to avoid taking bold climate action, it is all slipping away,” Getty said. “CEF supports nonviolent disruptive climate protest because it is the fastest way to create transformative change.”
One of the activists in handcuffs last week was Phoebe Plummer, 21, from London, who threw soup on a Van Gogh. “This is a proportionate response,” she said. “I’m not a criminal — I’m a scared little kid trying to fight for my future.”
She said the soup had been destined for Andy Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup Cans, but the activists settled on Van Gogh, reckoning it would get a bigger reaction. “I definitely did feel scared. But nothing scares me more than the future we’re facing.” Plummer joined Just Stop Oil in August. “It was the first thing that gave me hope in a really long time,” she said.
The group has been criticised for being largely white and middle-class. Dr Sophia Hatzisavvidou, a lecturer at Bath University specialising in climate change and environmental justice, said: “A diverse membership is important in terms of effectiveness. Policies change when an activist can approach a politician to say: my support comes from a very wide range of people.”
Plummer does not deny her privileged position. “I’m lucky,” she said. “I am a young white girl, I don’t face the worst of police brutality.”
Dr Ben Caldecott, director of the Oxford Sustainable Finance Group, criticised Just Stop Oil’s approach: “Civil disobedience of this kind is deeply counterproductive . . . ordinary people are being put off and it’s making it harder for people to make progress with a universal, collective cause.”
He believed that wealthy philanthropists could “achieve better outcomes” in other ways.
“The evidence suggests otherwise,” said a Just Stop Oil spokesman. “The history of non-violent civil resistance proves it is the most effective strategy for achieving the response required to protect our freedoms, rights and democracy.”@MeganAgnewhttps://twitter.com/meganagnew?lang=en

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/thou.title: Just Stop Oil activists throw tomato soup over Van Gogh masterpiece
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/thou.subtitle: Thousands to join Extinction Rebellion’s long weekend of protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/thou.text:
Environmental activists threw soup at a masterpiece by Vincent Van Gogh in the National Gallery during a day of protests in London yesterday.
Phoebe Plumber, 21, and Anna Holland, 20, are being investigated on suspicion of criminal damage and aggravated trespass after emptying two cans of tomato soup over Sunflowers, which is valued at more than £72 million.
The activists had been arrested many times before, including at protests in the past week, The Times has learnt. Both had been arrested at Just Stop Oil demonstrations and road blockades.
Paint was also thrown over the sign at Scotland Yard’s headquarters yesterday. Lora Johnson, one of the activists arrested over the incident, had been detained six days earlier for blocking Waterloo Bridge.
Yesterday a combined protest with Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion in central London attracted about 1,000 people and was peaceful, but the Metropolitan Police arrested 24 people on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage after paint was sprayed on the sign at the force’s headquarters in Westminster.
• Read more: Police will be ‘more assertive’ if Just Stop Oil protest crosses line, says Met chief
Johnson, 38, from Suffolk, said she did it to draw attention to five fellow activists in prison. A video of her went viral last Sunday when she was carried off Waterloo Bridge by police officers.
The Metropolitan Police are struggling to stop repeat offenders because prosecutors require a full case file, requiring statements and video evidence, before making a charging decision for offences such as obstruction of the highway. The force has made hundreds of arrests during Just Stop Oil’s 14-day campaign, meaning it could take weeks to finalise cases and leaving protesters free to attend further demonstrations.
Agencies including Transport for London are under pressure to seek civil injunctions to thwart the protesters.
Just Stop Oil, which is campaigning for the government to halt new fossil fuel licences, was widely condemned for the National Gallery stunt, and even fellow environmental campaigners warned they were undermining their cause.
Video of the incident showed visitors gasping “Oh my gosh” and calling for security as Plummer and Holland threw the soup at Sunflowers then glued themselves to the wall. Plummer said: “What is worth more, art or life? Are you more concerned about the protection of a painting or the protection of our planet and people?”
The gallery said the frame suffered minor damage but the 1888 painting was unscathed because it is covered in glass. It was back on display by the end of the day.
Plummer, a University of Manchester graduate from London, and Holland, who studied creative writing at Newcastle University, have repeatedly attended the group’s protests.
Plummer was detained on October 9 at Piccadilly Circus when she placed a bike lock around her neck and attached herself to a fellow protester. Three days before that she had been dragged off by the police at Trafalgar Square after she was unglued from the tarmac.
Friends said Holland had been arrested three times at protests before, including at a demonstration in Knightsbridge on Tuesday. Her friend Alex De Koning, 24, a Phd student, said she joined Just Stop Oil after becoming disillusioned with what she saw as the tame tactics of Extinction Rebellion.
Both groups are planning a weekend of resistance.
Commander Karen Findlay, the Met’s lead for public order, told The Times that officers would be able to remove and arrest protesters quickly because the “cumulative effect” of more than a fortnight of demonstrations would meet the legal threshold of serious disruption.
• The Times view on policing Just Stop Oil protests: Just Stop This
She said, however, that the Met could not just “hoick people off the road”.
Findlay said if the Met moved too quickly and disrupted protests without the proper legal authority, future prosecutions would collapse and the force could face judicial reviews. “That would do nothing for public confidence, and it would give the perception these people can act with impunity,” she said.
De-bonding. That’s my tip for word of the year. As in, “officers are now de-bonding them” (Laura Freeman writes). At just after 11am on Friday morning, two bone-headed bonders from the protest group Just Stop Oil entered Room 43 of the National Gallery, threw tins of Heinz tomato soup on Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and glued themselves to the wall. They have been arrested. The statement doesn’t say whether they were charged in situ or having been prised from the scene. They might have had the decency to make it Campbell’s Cream of Celery and allowed us an Andy Warhol joke.
On it goes. In July protesters covered John Constable’s blameless The Hay Wain with a poster imagining “a nightmare scene that demonstrates how oil will destroy our countryside”. A few days later a new group of numpties stuck themselves to a copy of Leonardo da Vinci’s Last Supper at the Royal Academy and sprayed “no new oil” on the wall below. Is it oil paint or petrol they object to? JMW Turner’s Thomson’s Aeolian Harp at Manchester Art Gallery, Vincent van Gogh’s Peach Trees in Blossom at the Courtauld in London and Horatio McCulloch’s My Heart’s in the Highlands at the Kelvingrove in Glasgow have all had the sticky-fingers treatment. At least so far, the protesters have confined themselves to the frames.
What riles me most is that these are fundamentally destructive, disruptive, uncreative acts. Meanwhile, my Instagram feed is awash with artists grinding natural pigments from plants, weaving baskets from brambles, making mosaics from chips of flowerbed china. All sorts of inventive zero-waste art. The Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall installation unveiled by Cecilia Vicuña this week uses clay pipes, pot shards and oyster shells mudlarked from the shores of the Thames.
If the Just Stop Oil lot must stick themselves to something, why not the Frieze Art Fair in Regent’s Park? Shame on Frieze for its endless trundle of lorries, its buyers and dealers flying in from abroad, its installations shipped round the world.
The Sunflowers — thank god and Gogh — are protected by glass, so no harm done. Still, I wish they’d Just Stop It. Or if they must protest, that they’d find an (un)worthier target.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/history/arti.title: This month in The Times photographic archive: October 2022
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/history/arti.text:
Sacked after serving just 38 days, Kwasi Kwarteng was the second-shortest serving chancellor in postwar history. He was beaten to this honour only by Conservative chancellor Iain Macleod, who lasted 30 days in Ted Heath’s Treasury in 1970, before his sudden death from a heart attack. In this photograph Macleod is shown working on his election campaign for Enfield West in 1950, a seat he went on to hold for 20 years.
Macleod is credited with inventing the phrase “stagflation” — economic stagnation and high inflation happening at the same time. Under the headline “Tory attack on stagflation”, The Times reported how Macleod coined the term in an attack on the Harold Wilson Government. “We have moved into a period of what I call ‘stagflation’,” he said in November 1965. “The cost of living has gone up by five points in ten months. We have lost one-third more days in industrial disputes. We have cut the road programme and many other vital investment programmes in the social services. For most of that period, we have seen all forms of national savings doing less well than a year ago. The value of the pound in that period has dropped by a shilling. We have suffered an intense and prolonged credit squeeze. We have a formidable load of debt.”
Liz Truss resigned after 44 days, making her the shortest-serving prime minister. George Canning, with 119 days, is now relegated to second place. A search of the archive identified one of the more recent prime ministers on the leaderboard. The Conservative leader Andrew Bonar Law served for 209 days, making him the fourth shortest-serving prime minister. He resigned in May 1923 due to ill health, and died of throat cancer six months later. The photograph is one of our few surviving images of him, meeting the French prime minister Raymond Poincaré in 1922.
Climate activists from Just Stop Oil shut down the Queen Elizabeth II bridge at the Dartford Crossing this month, causing two days of severe disruption.
The chief sports photographer at The Times, Marc Aspland, climbed the northwest pylon in 1991 as the bridge was being completed. He captured the view from 137 metres above water level for an exclusive set of images.
The BBC celebrated its centenary this month. A recently digitised image of Broadcasting House shows the building lit up at night in 1938. The first purpose-built home for radio broadcasting, it was designed by George Val Myer and built in 1932. With its curved front section and a clock tower topped by a large aerial mast, the building has been compared to a ship.
To celebrate their centenary the BBC opened their vast archives, sharing early broadcasts by journalists and presenters who went on to become household names.
Last month we featured photographs by William Horton taken on the royal tour to South Africa in 1947. One BBC figure was also on that trip and was captured by Horton broadcasting from his makeshift radio studio on board HMS Vanguard. Frank Gillard was a highly regarded war correspondent who became the director of BBC Radio and founded the oral history collection at the BBC. Famous for his reports from the Normandy landings and Germany on VE Day, The Times described Gillard as one of “ the best known voices on wartime radio” in his obituary in 1998.
The bicentary of The Sunday Times this month was a welcome excuse to unearth some highlights from the paper’s photographic history.
• The Sunday Times: the first 200 years
A young newspaper seller is photographed in 1957 wearing a Sunday Times apron. A bill for the latest edition advertises the serialisation of Archibald The Arctic by Archibald Fleming.
A 1955 billboard in Cranbourn Street, off Leicester Square in central London, previews the serialisation of Roger Bannister’s book First Four Minutes telling the story of the record-breaking “four minute mile” man.
A scene from 1960 captures the Piccadilly advertising boards in London alongside advertisements by Coca-Cola and Guinness. The story by Dame Rebecca West, a writer who was best known for her reports from the Nuremberg trials of Nazi war criminals, was a special investigation for The Sunday Times from South Africa.
The magazine section, launched in 1958, separated the arts, reviews and books content from the main paper, making The Sunday Times the first two-section paper in the UK. The headline “Discord in Whitehall” could have been written this week, but was an instalment from Field Marshal Montgomery’s memoirs serialised in the paper. The Sunday Times Colour Magazine followed in 1962, becoming the first colour newspaper supplement launched in the UK. Featuring famous artists and writers and pioneering the photojournalism of Don McCullin, among others, it was a significant step in the history of the newspaper. An image from 1963 shows a billboard to promote the colour magazine: “unique/complete/and it’s part of the paper”.
The Sunday Times Colour Magazine commissioned some of the world’s most famous photographers. The newspaper also employed a number of eminent staffers including Michael Ward, Frank Herrmann and Sally Soames. A lesser known figure perhaps was that of Kelvin Brodie. Known on Fleet Street as “Steve”, Brodie joined The Sunday Times in 1961 as a news photographer and became picture editor in 1976. His fifteen years as a photographer captured some iconic figures from the cultural and political life of the Sixties, including the last images of Malcolm X in the UK just days before his assasination, John Lennon and Yoko and the Rolling Stones. One politician developed a good working relationship with Brodie. The Times noted in his obituary that he was “Sir Harold Wilson’s favourite photographer, his was a famous shot of the former prime minister in Downing Street with a halo of tobacco smoke”.
Another Sunday Times photographer, Bryan Wharton, wrote that Brodie “was a brilliant photographer whose recent years as a largely desk-bound executive were often filled with a longing to return to photographic assignments”. It noted how his “brusque exterior hid a warm and generous character”. His burly physique no doubt proved useful in his 1965 assignment to photograph the notorious Kray twins, Ronnie and Reggie, at their family home in Bethnal Green. His lens photographed all the big names in the music scene; here the Beatles are photographed returning from their first US trip in 1964 to 4,000 adoring fans. The image of Georgie Fame backstage in 1965 also reveals Brodie at work, his reflection captured in the mirror.
With The Times and Sunday Times Cheltenham Literature Festival taking place this month, it felt appropriate to delve into the archive for images of people reading. These two photographs were taken for a Sunday Times holiday reading guide in 1974. The Ingenious Mr Stone by Robert Player was a popular choice.
The dramatic lighting in this 1936 image of a family reading by the fireplace was probably achieved by the photographer, Eddie Taylor, using a hidden light source to enhance the natural firelight.
National Adoption Week took place this month, highlighting the 3,000 children in need of an adoptive family in the UK. These photographs were taken at an adoption shop run by Family Finders in Chelmsford, Essex, in 1982. The Sunday Times headline was “The boy in the window: all he wants is a family”.“Barry” was a 12-year-old whose parents had died when he was three and who ended up back in the care system after his adoptive parents separated. He is photographed in the shop window, with his advertising board that he helped decorate describing himself to passers-by. It is a poignant if unsettling image captured by Sally Soames.
After lying derelict for decades, the regenerated Battersea Power Station has opened its doors to the public for the first time in its history.
A gallery of images was scanned from the archive to show the structure through the ages including this shot from 1931, a wonderful silhouette taken as the power station was being built.
The new Rolls-Royce Spectre marks a turning point for the luxury car maker as its first fully electric car.
The Times outlined how before even meeting Henry Royce, Charles Rolls had experienced an electric car and grasped its huge potential. His ride in a Columbia Electric Carriage and comments in an American motoring magazine have been unearthed 122 years later: “The electric car is perfectly noiseless and clean. There is no smell or vibration. They should become very useful when fixed charging stations can be arranged.” If it took longer than he expected, the Spectre is a step towards fulfilling Rolls’s prophecy. This image from The Times Motoring Survey published in 1964 featured a Phantom V getting a valet service, the headlights flanking the emblematic Parthenon-style radiator grille.
In Black History Month three granddaughters of Jack Leslie, a footballer from the 1920s, unveiled a crowd-funded statue of their grandfather outside the Plymouth Argyle stadium. Leslie was the first black player to be selected for England, in October 1925. Named as one of the substitutes in the 13-man squad to play Ireland, he was mysteriously dropped before the squad travelled and was never picked again. On the day that the statue, by Andy Edwards, was unveiled, Debbie Hewitt, the FA chairwoman, said that Leslie would be awarded a posthumous honorary cap “to right the historical wrong”. The Jack Leslie Campaign, run by two Plymouth Argyle fans, Greg Foxsmith and Matt Tiller, contacted The Times in late 2020 and the Times’s photograph is now on the plinth outside Home Park, where these photographs were taken in 1932.
Dame Angela Lansbury died this month, aged 96. The three-time Oscar-nominated actress was best known for playing the novelist and amateur sleuth Jessica Fletcher in Murder, She Wrote. Her first marriage ended in divorce within a year, but our earliest surviving images capture her wedding, in 1949, to Peter Shaw. Both previously married, they were refused a wedding by the Church of England and were married by the Church of Scotland. Their marriage endured 54 years until her husband’s death in 2003.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/anti-oi.title: Police will be ‘more assertive’ if Just Stop Oil protest crosses line, says Met chief
https://www.thetimes.com/article/anti-oi.text:
Police have not fully clamped down on the Just Stop Oil protesters because their road blockages in London have not caused “serious disruption”, Scotland Yard’s commissioner has said.
Sir Mark Rowley said he was frustrated by the protest campaign, now in its 12th day, but the disruption had not met the legal threshold of disruption, which would allow officers to be more assertive.
Just Stop Oil protesters yesterday delayed an ambulance, a fire engine and cars carrying babies to hospital after they blocked traffic in west London. Drivers have taken action by dragging protesters from blockades.
Rowley said that police had made 338 arrests, mainly of supporters of Just Stop Oil along with some from Animal Rebellion. But although “enormous” policing resources were being directed at the protest movement, he said it was not yet disruptive enough for a significant clampdown. He said the Met was in contact several times a day with Transport for London, councils and the emergency services to check the level of disruption.
Rowley told the London Assembly’s police and crime committee: “Over the last 11 days, all of those partners have been of a view that it doesn’t cause serious disruption. As soon as we have evidence of that serious disruption either being crossed as a line, or a good prospect of it being crossed, we’ll start being more assertive with our powers.”
He said the protests had to meet the legal threshold of causing “serious disruption to the life of the community”. Until that point, police powers such as arresting for obstruction of the highway could not be used because the protests were lawful. He said: “If my officers are to make legal intervention, they have to stand it on some evidence that is reasonable. Frustratingly that’s the situation we’re in.”
It is understood that in the event that the protests reach the serious disruption threshold, the Met will be able to move in more quickly and make more arrests. Currently officers must allow lawful protest and will only make arrests for obstruction of the highway if there is an effort to cause damage to business or block roads for lengthy periods.
Asked about gridlocked roads, Rowley said: “The law is very clear that just blocking a road in itself isn’t automatically serious disruption.”
Susan Hall, the Conservative chairwoman of the committee, said she had been appalled by the disruption and claimed that police officers had handed cups of tea to protesters. Rowley said he was not aware of that and added: “I hope we’re not doing that, I agree with you it’s not our responsibility.”
The Met’s response over the 11 days of protests has been the equivalent of about 2,156 officer days.
Rowley said: “That’s an enormous amount of policing resources that aren’t tackling issues that matter to local communities, aren’t dealing with knife crime, aren’t dealing with violence against women and girls.”
Suella Braverman, the home secretary, has said she expects police to use the “full powers” given to them by the government after fossil fuel protesters reportedly obstructed a fire engine and an ambulance. Braverman branded the actions of demonstrators from Just Stop Oil in west London as “self-defeating” and “completely indefensible”.
Videos shared online this week show a fire engine and an ambulance with blue lights on unable to get through traffic after 32 protesters — some glueing themselves to the road — blocked three routes in Knightsbridge and Brompton Road in London. Just Stop Oil, which is calling on the government to halt all new fossil fuel projects, said it had paused its blockade to let a fire engine through.
